title: Pages, tuples and heap files
goal: By the end you can explain why an engine that updates data in place stores a table as fixed-size pages, read a PostgreSQL heap page with pageinspect, explain how a slotted page keeps variable-length rows behind slot ids that never change, and build one that inserts, deletes and compacts.

warmup.q: A PostgreSQL row sits at ctid (0,4), page 0, slot 4. You delete the rows in slots 2 and 3 of the same page and run a plain `VACUUM`. What is the row's ctid now?
options: (0,2), because the remaining rows slide up to fill the gap
Still (0,4): VACUUM may move the row's bytes inside the page, but never its slot number
A new page, because VACUUM moves rows off pages that have holes
Every ctid changes, because VACUUM rewrites the whole table file
warmup.why: Indexes store (page, slot), so the slot number must not change while the row lives. VACUUM compacts the page by moving row bytes and updating the slot's offset; in the Try it below, the row in slot 4 moves from byte 8000 to byte 8096 and stays in slot 4. The last option describes `VACUUM FULL`, which rewrites the table into a new file under an exclusive lock. Plain VACUUM doesn't.

sections.h: A table is a file of 8 KB pages
sections.body:
Lesson 1's store kept one log file and every key in RAM. A table needs more. A ledger can hold a billion rows, far more than fit in memory. Rows get updated and deleted. And an index must be able to point at a row and find it again later. This lesson starts the second family of engines from lesson 1, the kind that keeps data in fixed-size pages and changes those pages where they lie. So start from scratch: how should rows sit in a file?

The hardware answers the first part. Drives and the kernel move data in blocks, never single bytes (lesson 1 of this track showed 4 KB and 16 KB pages). So a database cuts every table file into fixed-size **pages** and always reads and writes a whole page. PostgreSQL's page is 8 KB, 8,192 bytes. Page 0 is bytes 0 to 8,191 of the file, page 1 the next 8,192 bytes, and page `n` always starts at byte `n x 8192`. To read one row you read its page. The page is also what the cache in the next lesson holds.

Insert 1,000 small ledger rows into a new PostgreSQL table and look at its file: 57,344 bytes, exactly 7 pages. PostgreSQL stores each table as its own file under its data directory, the folder where the server keeps everything (`base/<database id>/<file number>`), and grows it one page at a time. A table over 1 GB is split into several 1 GB files, but it is still one numbered array of pages.

Now every row can have an address: which page, and which row inside that page. PostgreSQL calls it the **ctid** and writes it `(page, item)`. `(0,1)` is the first row on page 0. In the Try it, rows 1 to 157 fill page 0 and row 158 starts page 1 at `(1,1)`. An index (lesson 4 builds one, and lesson 7 reads the plans that use it) is a separate structure that maps a column value to a ctid. So a row's item number must not change while the row stays on its page, or every index entry pointing at it breaks. The figure shows this picture: a numbered array of pages, and inside each page a slot array pointing at rows. The next section shows how a page keeps the promise.

PostgreSQL's table file is a **heap**: rows go wherever there is room, in no particular order. That raises a practical question. Which page has room for the next insert? Checking every page of a 100 GB table, 13 million pages, for each insert is out of the question. So PostgreSQL keeps a small side file, the **free space map**, that records roughly how many free bytes each page has. An insert asks it for a page with enough room, and only when no page has room does PostgreSQL add a new page at the end of the file. You'll see it work in the third Try it, when a new row lands in space freed on page 0 instead of on a new page 7.

try.title: Find a table's pages
steps: From `labs/`, start PostgreSQL with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait` and open psql with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`.
Predict: 1,000 rows of three small columns. How many 8 KB pages?
Paste the block below. The second query pulls the page number out of each row's ctid and counts rows per page. The last line runs `ls` inside the container on the table's file.

code.title: psql

try.expect:
Seven pages: 157 rows on each of pages 0 to 5 and 58 on page 6. Row 157 is `(0,157)` and row 158 is `(1,1)`:

```text
       file       | bytes
------------------+-------
 base/16384/17600 | 57344

  ctid   | id  | account | amount_cents
---------+-----+---------+--------------
 (0,1)   |   1 | acct-1  |          100

```

The file number (17600 here) differs on your machine. `ls -l` shows the same 57,344 bytes. The next sections explain why exactly 157 rows fit.

sections.h: A slotted page: pointers at the front, rows at the back
sections.body:
Rows have different lengths. A ledger row with account `acct-1` takes 48 bytes; one with a 500-character memo takes over 500. So how do you place them in an 8 KB page and find row 4 again quickly?

Version 1 packs them back to back from the start of the page. To find row 4, you read row 1's length, skip it, read row 2's length, skip it, and so on. That is slow but it works, until you delete row 2. Either you leave a hole, which every later walk has to recognise and skip, or you slide rows 3 onwards down to close it, and every one of those rows is now at a different byte offset.

Version 2 puts a small array at the start of the page: entry 4 holds row 4's offset and length, so finding it is one lookup, and a row can move as long as its entry is updated. But how big is the array? A fixed size caps the number of rows per page. And if the rows start right after the array, the array can't grow without moving every row.

Version 3 fixes that by letting the two grow toward each other. This is the **slotted page**, and PostgreSQL, SQLite and Oracle all use it:

- a small header at the start of the page,
- an array of slots (PostgreSQL calls them **line pointers**) right after it, one per row, each holding the row's offset and length,
- the rows themselves, packed from the end of the page backwards,
- free space in the middle.

The header keeps two offsets. `pd_lower` is where the slot array ends and `pd_upper` is where the rows begin. An insert copies the row in just below `pd_upper`, adds a slot just after `pd_lower`, and moves both toward each other. The page is full when they would cross. Free space is always one gap in the middle, whatever sizes the rows have.

PostgreSQL's numbers, from its page layout docs: a 24-byte page header, 4-byte line pointers, and an optional special area at the very end that heap pages don't use. In the Try it, page 0 of `ledger` has `lower = 652` and `upper = 656`. That is 24 bytes of header plus 157 line pointers of 4 bytes, then 4 free bytes, then 157 rows of 48 bytes reaching to byte 8,192. The page is full: one more 48-byte row needs 52 bytes with its line pointer.

The slot array is a level of indirection, and what it buys is this: **a row's slot number never changes while the row lives**, even when its bytes move. An index entry says "page 0, slot 4". The page can rearrange its bytes freely, as long as it updates slot 4's offset. The stepper shows this on the 4 KB page you build in the lab.

steps: In the same psql session, predict `lower` and `upper` for page 0 from what you know: 24-byte header, 157 rows, 4-byte line pointers, 48-byte rows.
Run the two queries below. `get_raw_page` copies the 8 KB page; `page_header` and `heap_page_items` decode it. The image creates the pageinspect extension when the database starts.

try.expect:
```text
 lower | upper | special | pagesize
-------+-------+---------+----------
   652 |   656 |    8192 |     8192

 lp  | lp_off | lp_flags | lp_len | t_hoff
-----+--------+----------+--------+--------
   1 |   8144 |        1 |     48 |     24
   2 |   8096 |        1 |     48 |     24

```

`lower` is 24 + 157 x 4 = 652. Row 1 sits at the very end of the page and each next row 48 bytes lower, until row 157 starts at 656, which is `upper`. `special = 8192` means the special space is empty. `lp_flags = 1` means the slot is in normal use.

sections.h: Delete leaves a hole, and compaction closes it
sections.body:
Delete row 2 from a full page. What should happen to its 48 bytes?

The simplest answer is to remove them at once and slide the neighbours over the gap. PostgreSQL can't do that, for a reason the Transactions track's lesson on MVCC explains in full: a query that started before your DELETE must still be able to read row 2 until it finishes. So at DELETE time PostgreSQL only writes the deleting transaction's id (every transaction gets a number) into the row's **`t_xmax`** field ("deleted by"). Run `DELETE FROM ledger WHERE id IN (2, 3)` and look at page 0: rows 2 and 3 are still there, same offsets, same length, with `t_xmax` set.

The space comes back later through **VACUUM**, PostgreSQL's cleanup command, which the autovacuum background process runs for you. Once no running query can still need the dead rows, VACUUM does two things you can see on the page:

1. The line pointers of rows 2 and 3 become unused: offset 0, length 0, `lp_flags = 0`.
2. The page is compacted. Row 4 moves from byte 8,000 to byte 8,096, right below row 1, and `upper` rises from 656 to 752. That is 96 more bytes of contiguous free space, two rows' worth.

Row 4 is still `(0,4)`. Its bytes moved and its slot didn't, which is the reason the slot array exists. The table file is still 57,344 bytes: VACUUM makes space reusable inside the file, and it only gives space back to the operating system when whole pages at the very end of the file are empty.

Then insert a new row, and it lands at `(0,2)`, in a slot VACUUM just freed. Reusing a slot number is dangerous: if an old index entry still said "page 0, slot 2", a lookup would find the new row instead of nothing. PostgreSQL reuses a slot only after VACUUM has removed every index entry pointing at it. This table has no index, so VACUUM could mark the slots unused straight away. With an index, a dead slot first waits in a dead state (`lp_flags = 3`) until the index entries are gone.

Your lab page is simpler and stricter. It has no VACUUM and no indexes to clean, so it never reuses a slot number. A deleted slot stays dead for the life of the page, and compaction moves bytes but leaves every slot where it is.

try.title: Watch VACUUM compact a page
steps: Delete two rows and look at the first four slots. Predict before each query: what changes?
Run `VACUUM`, then look at the header and the slots again.
Check the file size, then insert one row and note its ctid.

code.title: psql

try.expect:
After the DELETE, rows 2 and 3 are untouched except for `t_xmax`:

```text
 lp | lp_off | lp_flags | lp_len | t_xmin | t_xmax
----+--------+----------+--------+--------+--------
  1 |   8144 |        1 |     48 |    857 |      0
  2 |   8096 |        1 |     48 |    857 |    858
  3 |   8048 |        1 |     48 |    857 |    858
  4 |   8000 |        1 |     48 |    857 |      0
```

After VACUUM, `upper` is 752 (up from 656), slots 2 and 3 are empty and row 4 has moved:

```text

----+--------+----------+--------+--------+--------
  1 |   8144 |        1 |     48 |    857 |      0
  2 |      0 |        0 |      0 |        |
  3 |      0 |        0 |      0 |        |
  4 |   8096 |        1 |     48 |    857 |      0
```

The file is still 57,344 bytes, and the new row comes back as `(0,2)`. Your transaction ids differ.

sections.h: Every row carries a header, and big values move out of the page
sections.body:
Two questions are left from the Try its. Why does a row holding two numbers and a 6-character string take 48 bytes? And what happens to a row too big for an 8 KB page?

The figure takes row 1 apart. The first 24 bytes are the **tuple header** (PostgreSQL calls a stored row a tuple): 23 bytes of fields plus one byte of padding. The fields you'll meet again are `t_xmin` (the transaction that inserted the row), `t_xmax` (the one that deleted or replaced it, 0 if none) and `t_ctid` (this row's own address, or the address of a newer version of it). The columns follow: `id` takes 8 bytes, `'acct-1'` takes 7 (a 1-byte length plus 6 characters), then 1 byte of padding so that `amount_cents` starts at an offset divisible by 8 (PostgreSQL aligns 8-byte values that way so the CPU can read them in one go), then 8 bytes for the amount.

So half of this row is overhead, and each row also costs a 4-byte line pointer. Narrow tables pay the most: a table of two `int` columns spends 28 bytes per row on header and slot before any data. Count it when you estimate how big a table will get.

Now the big row. The simplest idea is to let it spill over into the next page. That breaks the model this lesson built: a slot can only point inside its own page, and reading one row could take several page reads. So a row must fit in one page, and your lab page enforces a stricter version: it refuses any record bigger than a quarter of the page.

PostgreSQL keeps rows small with **TOAST**. When a row is wider than about 2 KB, it works on the row's biggest values. First it tries to compress them. If the row is still too wide, it moves values out of line into a separate TOAST table, cut into chunks of about 2,000 bytes (four chunks fit on one page), and leaves an 18-byte pointer in the row. A single value can be up to 1 GB this way.

The Try it shows both outcomes. A 20,000-character string of one repeated letter compresses to 241 bytes and stays in the row. A 12,800-character string of hex digits barely compresses, so it moves out: the heap row shrinks to 46 bytes (24 of header, 4 for the `int`, 18 for the pointer) and the text lives in seven TOAST chunks. Reading that column means reading those chunks too. `SELECT id FROM receipts` never touches them, while `SELECT *` does, which is one honest reason to name your columns.

try.title: Push a value out to TOAST
steps: Create a table and insert one long, compressible value and one long value that barely compresses (400 MD5 hashes in a row).
Predict which one stays in the heap page.
Compare each value's length with its stored size, look at the row lengths on page 0, then read the TOAST table's chunks.
When you are done with this lesson, stop and delete the database: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v`.

code.title: psql

try.expect:
```text
 id | chars | stored_bytes
----+-------+--------------
  1 | 20000 |          241
  2 | 12800 |        12800

 lp | lp_len
----+--------
  1 |    269
  2 |     46
```

Row 1 was compressed and stays inline (269 bytes with its header). Row 2 is a 46-byte stub with an 18-byte pointer. The TOAST table holds its text in chunks 0 to 5 of 1,996 bytes each and a last chunk of 824 bytes: 12,800 bytes in all.

analogy: A slotted page works like a filing drawer with a numbered card list stuck inside the front. Card 4 says where folder 4 sits in the drawer. When you pull out two folders and push the rest together to close the gap, you correct the positions written on the cards, but card 4 is still card 4, so anyone who noted "drawer 0, card 4" still finds the folder. The analogy breaks on space: a real card list doesn't eat into the drawer, but on a page the slot array and the rows grow toward each other and compete for the same 8 KB.
in_your_world: Oracle uses the same design. An Oracle data block (8 KB by default on most platforms) has a block header, a row directory and row data that fills from the bottom up, and a ROWID contains the row's slot number inside its block, just like a ctid. In PostgreSQL the knowledge pays off on wide payment tables. A `payload jsonb` column holding a 6 KB card-network response is TOASTed, so a report that runs `SELECT *` over a million authorizations reads every TOAST chunk, while `SELECT id, amount_cents, status` reads only heap pages. And a ledger table with three small columns pays more in tuple headers than in data, which is worth knowing when you estimate how much disk a year of rows will take.
mistake: The common mistake is expecting a DELETE, or a plain VACUUM, to make the table smaller on disk. People delete 40 million expired idempotency keys, watch the disk graph and see nothing change. DELETE only marks rows dead. VACUUM makes their space reusable for new rows inside the same file, and only gives back completely empty pages at the end of the file. That is usually what you want, because new rows will fill the space. If you really need the disk back, `VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table into a new file, but it holds an exclusive lock for the whole rewrite, so plan it like a migration.

compare.title: PostgreSQL heap page vs SQLite b-tree page

a.label: PostgreSQL heap page
a.title: 8 KB
a.src:
24-byte page header (pd_lower, pd_upper, ...)
line pointers: 4 bytes each, in insertion order
  offset (15 bits), flags (2 bits), length (15 bits)
free space
tuples, packed from the end of the page
special space (empty for heap pages)

row address: ctid = (page, line pointer number)

b.label: SQLite table b-tree page
b.title: page size: a power of two, 512 to 65536
b.src:
8-byte header (leaf) or 12-byte header (interior)
cell pointers: 2 bytes each, sorted in key order
unallocated space
cell content, packed from the end of the page
  holes tracked as freeblocks and 1 to 3 byte fragments

row address: the rowid key, found through the b-tree

compare.note: Both are slotted pages: pointers at the front, content at the back, free space between. The difference is what the pointer order means. PostgreSQL's line pointers are in insertion order and a pointer's number is a stable address, so indexes can point straight at it. SQLite's cell pointers are kept sorted by key because the page is a node of a b-tree, so a cell's position in the array changes as other rows come and go, and rows are found by key instead.

worked.title: Decode a page from its header

steps.say: `page_header` says `lower = 652`, `upper = 656` for an 8 KB heap page. Count the line pointers: the slot array runs from the end of the 24-byte header to `lower`, at 4 bytes per pointer.
Find the free space: it is the gap between the two offsets.
Find the average row size: the rows occupy everything from `upper` to the end of the page, because the special space is empty (`special = 8192`).
steps.code:
row bytes = 8192 - upper = 7536
per row   = 7536 / 157 = 48 bytes

steps.say: Decide whether one more 48-byte row fits. It needs its bytes plus a new line pointer, and only 4 bytes are free, so this page is full and the free space map sends the next insert elsewhere. The same check in the lab's page:

lab.title: Build a slotted page
steps: Open `SlottedPage.kt`. The header and slot helpers at the bottom (`lower`, `upper`, `slotOffset`, `slotLength`, `setSlot`) are done. Use them instead of raw buffer offsets.
Run the tests once. All 10 fail.
Write `freeSpace` (one line) and `get` (length 0 means a dead slot; check the slot id exists).
Write `insert`: reject empty and too-large records, then place the record just below `upper`, add the slot at `slotCount()`, and move `lower` and `upper`.
Write `delete` (mark the slot dead) and `compact` (slide live records to the end of the page, update their offsets and `upper`).
Make `insert` call `compact` when the holes would make room. Run the tests until all 10 pass.
hints: Free space after a compaction is `PAGE_SIZE - lower - (sum of live record lengths)`. Compare that with `record.size + SLOT_SIZE` to decide between compacting and returning null.

In `compact`, handle live records in order of descending offset (closest to the end first). Each one then moves only into space that is already free, and `System.arraycopy` on `buf.array()` is safe even when the source and target overlap.
`buf.put(index, bytes)` and `buf.get(index, bytes)` are absolute bulk copies; they don't touch the buffer's position.
The layout test reads the raw bytes: `lower` at offset 0, `upper` at offset 2, slot 0 at offset 4. If it fails while the others pass, check that the first record ends exactly at byte 4096.

drill.title: Write insert and compact from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Using only the helpers `lower`, `upper`, `slotOffset`, `slotLength`, `setSlot` and `slotCount`, write `insert` (with compaction when the holes help) and `compact` for a slotted page. Then check: does a record keep its slot id through `compact`?

recap: A PostgreSQL table is a heap: a file of 8 KB pages, with rows wherever there is room. The free space map points inserts at pages with space.
A slotted page keeps a header, an array of slots (line pointers) growing from the front, and rows packed from the back. Free space is the gap between `pd_lower` and `pd_upper`.
A row's address is (page, slot). The slot number stays fixed while the row lives, so compaction can move bytes without breaking indexes.
DELETE leaves the row in place with `t_xmax` set. VACUUM frees the slot and compacts the page, but the file does not shrink.
Each heap row costs a 24-byte header plus a 4-byte line pointer. Rows wider than about 2 KB get compressed or moved to a TOAST table in about 2,000-byte chunks.

quiz.q: Every row in a table is 120 bytes including its 24-byte header. About how many rows fit on one 8 KB PostgreSQL heap page?
quiz.why: The page has a 24-byte header, and each row needs its 120 bytes plus a 4-byte line pointer: (8192 - 24) / 124 = 65.9, so 65. 68 forgets the line pointers (8168 / 120). 85 counts only the 96 bytes of column data and forgets that every row carries its own header.

quiz.q: An index entry points at (page 12, slot 7). VACUUM then compacts page 12 and the row in slot 7 moves 300 bytes. What happens on the next index lookup?
options: The lookup fails until the index is rebuilt
VACUUM rewrote the index entry to the row's new byte offset
The lookup reads slot 7, which now holds the row's new offset, and finds the row
The row was moved to a new page, so the lookup follows a forwarding pointer
quiz.why: Indexes never store byte offsets, only (page, slot). Compaction moves the bytes and updates the slot's offset, so the same index entry keeps working without touching the index at all. That indirection is the reason slotted pages exist.

quiz.q: Your lab page has 36 bytes of contiguous free space and 300 bytes in holes left by deleted records. What should `insert` do with a 250-byte record?
options: Return null, because only 36 bytes are free
Put the record into the biggest hole
Reuse the slot of one of the deleted records
Compact the page first, then insert into the single 336-byte gap
quiz.why: The record needs 254 bytes (250 plus a 4-byte slot). After compaction the free gap is 36 + 300 = 336 bytes, so it fits. Splitting a record across holes isn't possible, and reusing a dead slot id would let an old index entry find the wrong record.

quiz.q: You store a 50 KB card-network response as `text` in an authorizations table, and it compresses poorly. What does the row on the heap page hold for that column?
options: An 18-byte pointer to chunks of about 2,000 bytes in the table's TOAST table
The full 50 KB, spread across seven consecutive heap pages
Nothing: PostgreSQL rejects rows larger than one page
The first 2 KB of the text, with the rest in the WAL
quiz.why: A row must fit in one page, so PostgreSQL compresses wide values and, if the row is still over about 2 KB, moves them out of line into the TOAST table and leaves an 18-byte pointer. Heap rows never span pages, and the WAL is a log of changes, not storage for column values.

quiz.q: From lesson 1: a transaction inserts a row, PostgreSQL appends the change to the WAL, and COMMIT returns. The 8 KB heap page with the new row is still only in memory when the server crashes. Is the row there after restart?
options: No, because the heap page was never written
Yes, because recovery replays the WAL and redoes the insert on the page
Only if a checkpoint had finished after the commit
Only if the table has a primary key
quiz.why: COMMIT returns only after the WAL up to the commit record is flushed. On restart, recovery replays WAL records from the last checkpoint and re-applies the insert to the page. That is why the database doesn't need to write data pages at commit time.

flashcards.front: What is a ctid in PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: A row's physical address: (page number, line pointer number). Indexes store it.

flashcards.front: What do `pd_lower` and `pd_upper` mark on a page?
flashcards.back: `pd_lower` is the end of the line pointer array; `pd_upper` is the start of the row data. The free space is between them.

flashcards.front: Why can compaction move rows without breaking indexes?
flashcards.back: Indexes point at (page, slot). Compaction moves the bytes and updates the slot's offset, so the slot number stays the same.

flashcards.front: What does a PostgreSQL DELETE do to the row on the page?
flashcards.back: Nothing physical. It sets the row's `t_xmax` to the deleting transaction. VACUUM reclaims the space later.

flashcards.front: How big is a PostgreSQL heap tuple header, and what does a line pointer cost?
flashcards.back: 23 bytes, padded to 24 when there are no nulls. Each row also needs a 4-byte line pointer.

flashcards.front: When does TOAST kick in, and what is left in the row?
flashcards.back: When a row is wider than about 2 KB. Big values are compressed and, if still too big, moved to the TOAST table in about 2,000-byte chunks; the row keeps an 18-byte pointer.

terms.plain: The fixed-size block (8 KB in PostgreSQL) a database reads, writes and caches as one unit.
A table file whose rows sit wherever there is room, in no order.
A page layout with an array of slots at the front pointing to variable-length rows packed at the back.
PostgreSQL's 4-byte slot: the row's offset, length and state.
A PostgreSQL row's physical address, (page, line pointer number).
A small side file that records roughly how much room each page has, so inserts can find one quickly.
PostgreSQL's way of storing big column values compressed or out of line in a separate table.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate why a PostgreSQL page keeps an array of line pointers instead of just packing rows one after another, and what would break if VACUUM renumbered the rows after compacting a page.
explain_back.answer: Rows have different lengths, so you can't find row 4 by multiplying 4 by a row size. The line pointer array gives each row a fixed-size slot that holds its offset and length, and indexes store (page, slot) rather than a byte offset. That lets the page move row bytes around, for example when VACUUM compacts away the holes left by deleted rows, as long as it updates the slot's offset. If VACUUM renumbered the rows instead, every index entry pointing at that page would suddenly point at the wrong row or at nothing, and you would have to rewrite the indexes every time a page was compacted.

deeper.body:
**Line pointer states.** `lp_flags` has four values: 0 unused, 1 normal, 2 redirect, 3 dead. You saw 0 and 1. A dead pointer (3) has lost its row but may still be referenced by index entries, so it can't be reused yet. A redirect (2) appears with **HOT updates** (heap-only tuples). When an UPDATE changes no indexed column and the new version fits on the same page, PostgreSQL writes the new version on that page and adds no new index entries. Later, page pruning turns the old version's pointer into a redirect to the new one, so the index entry still leads to the live row. HOT updates are much cheaper than ordinary ones, which must add an entry to every index.

**fillfactor.** For tables the default `fillfactor` is 100: inserts pack pages full. A heavily updated table, say an `account_balance` row rewritten on every payment, can be created `WITH (fillfactor = 80)` so each page keeps 20% free for HOT updates. You trade disk space for fewer index writes.

**Where the analogy with your lab stops.** The lab's page compacts whenever an insert needs the room. PostgreSQL prunes and defragments a heap page opportunistically when a query visits it and finds it nearly full, and during VACUUM, and it needs a cleanup lock (an exclusive lock held by the only process pinning the page) to move row bytes, because another backend could be holding a pointer straight into the page's memory. That pinning rule is part of the buffer pool, which is the next lesson.
